content: Anderson-Fabry disease is a genetic disorder linked to the X chromosome that results in a defect in glycosphingolipid metabolism. This condition leads to progressive renal insufficiency, which is a major cause of morbidity. Additional complications arise from cardiovascular and cerebrovascular involvement. Affected males and symptomatic female carriers experience reduced survival rates. This document is an updated Cochrane review, originally published in 2010 and previously updated in 2013, focusing on enzyme replacement therapy (ERT) for Anderson-Fabry disease. The objective of this review was to assess the effectiveness and safety of enzyme replacement therapy (ERT) compared to other interventions, placebo, or no intervention in treating Anderson-Fabry disease. The search for relevant studies included databases such as the Cystic Fibrosis and Genetic Disorders Group's Inborn Errors of Metabolism Trials Register (last searched on July 8, 2016), as well as Clinical Trials on The Cochrane Library, MEDLINE, Embase, and LILACS (last searched on September 24, 2015). The selection criteria included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving agalsidase alfa or beta in participants diagnosed with Anderson-Fabry disease. Two authors independently selected trials, assessed their methodological quality, and extracted data. Nine trials involving 351 participants met the inclusion criteria. These trials compared either agalsidase alfa or beta to placebo or to each other. Agalsidase Alfa vs. Placebo: Two trials reported on globotriaosylceramide (Gb3) concentrations in plasma and tissue, but the aggregate results were not statistically significant. One trial measured pain scores using the Brief Pain Inventory (BPI). Statistically significant improvements in pain severity were observed in participants receiving agalsidase alfa at up to three months (mean difference: -2.10; 95% CI: -3.79 to -0.41), up to five months (mean difference: -1.90; 95% CI: -3.65 to -0.15), and up to six months (mean difference: -2.00; 95% CI: -3.66 to -0.34). Pain-related quality of life also improved significantly at over five months and up to six months (mean difference: -2.10; 95% CI: -3.92 to -0.28), but no significant differences were observed at other time points. Death was not reported as an outcome in these trials. Agalsidase Beta vs. Placebo: One of the three trials reported on Gb3 concentrations in plasma and tissue, showing significant improvements in kidney (mean difference: -1.70; 95% CI: -2.09 to -1.31), heart (mean difference: -0.90; 95% CI: -1.18 to -0.62), and composite outcomes (renal, cardiac, cerebrovascular complications, and death; mean difference: -4.80; 95% CI: -5.45 to -4.15). No significant differences were observed between groups for mortality, and no trials reported on pain outcomes. Agalsidase Alfa vs. Agalsidase Beta: Two trials compared these two forms of ERT. One trial found no significant differences between the groups in terms of adverse events (risk ratio: 0.36; 95% CI: 0.08 to 1.59) or serious adverse events (risk ratio: 0.30; 95% CI: 0.03 to 2.57). Different Dosing Schedules of Agalsidase Alfa: Two trials evaluated different dosing regimens of agalsidase alfa. One trial compared three doses (0.2 mg/kg every two weeks, 0.1 mg/kg weekly, and 0.2 mg/kg weekly), while the other trial assessed two additional doses (0.4 mg/kg weekly and every other week). Neither trial demonstrated significant differences in Gb3 levels, self-assessed health state, or pain scores across the dosing schedules. Safety: One trial comparing agalsidase alfa to agalsidase beta found no significant differences in adverse events, such as dyspnea or hypertension. However, adverse events like rigors and fever were more common with agalsidase beta compared to placebo. The methodological quality of the included trials was generally unclear, particularly regarding random sequence generation and allocation concealment. Conclusions: Trials comparing enzyme replacement therapy to placebo demonstrated significant improvements in microvascular endothelial deposits of Gb3 and pain-related quality of life. However, there is no evidence to suggest whether agalsidase alfa or beta is superior, nor is there clarity on the optimal dose or frequency of ERT. Adverse events were more frequent with agalsidase beta compared to placebo. The long-term effects of ERT on morbidity and mortality associated with Anderson-Fabry disease remain uncertain. This review underscores the need for further research into the use of enzyme replacement therapy for this condition.
